opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot, and I think the intuition most people have is that you should start in commercial settings: warehouses, factories, logistics, because the environments are more structured, the tasks are more repetitive, and the economics are easier to justify. And there's a lot of truth to that. But I think the case for homes is underrated, for a few reasons.

The first is data. What's really bottlenecking robotics right now isn't so much the hardware or even the model architectures. It's the diversity of experience the robot is learning from. A warehouse is, by design, a very narrow distribution. You can get a robot to be extremely good at picking a certain class of boxes off a certain kind of shelf, but that doesn't teach it very much about the world. Homes are the opposite. Every kitchen is different, every person organizes their laundry differently, the lighting changes, there are kids and pets and clutter. That messiness is exactly what you need if your goal is a general-purpose robot rather than a specialized machine. If you believe, like I do, that the path to capable robots looks a lot like the path to capable language models, scale plus diversity, then homes are where the richest data lives.

The second is the size of the opportunity. Domestic labor is enormous. Cooking, cleaning, tidying, laundry, caring for elderly family members: billions of hours a year, mostly unpaid, disproportionately falling on women. If you can take even a fraction of that off people's plates, the impact on quality of life is huge, and so is the market.

The third is about tolerance for imperfection. This sounds counterintuitive, but in a commercial setting you're usually competing against a very optimized human workflow with tight throughput requirements. If your robot succeeds 90% of the time, that's often a non-starter. In a home, if a robot folds most of your laundry and occasionally leaves a shirt for you, that's still a win. People are surprisingly forgiving when something is helping them with chores they hate. So you can get into the loop earlier, start collecting real-world data earlier, and improve from there.

Now, I don't want to be naive about it. Homes are harder in real ways. Safety is a much bigger deal when you have children and elderly people around. Privacy is a serious concern, because you're putting cameras and microphones into the most intimate space people have. Cost has to come way down for consumer adoption. And reliability expectations will rise once the novelty wears off. So I don't think it's an either/or. Commercial deployments can fund the company and harden the hardware, but if you only ever deploy in narrow industrial settings, I worry you end up optimizing for a local maximum and never get to the generalist robot.

So my view is: if your ambition is general-purpose embodied intelligence, you eventually have to go where the world is messiest, and that's the home. The question is really about sequencing and doing it responsibly, not whether.

r001.rationale: The response says home environments offer the diverse experience needed to improve general-purpose robots and that earlier home deployment can collect real-world data sooner.

r002.rationale: It calls home safety a bigger concern because children and elderly people may be present, but does not present this as a reason homes may be among the last settings for deployment.

r003.rationale: It says cost must fall for consumer adoption, but does not connect that constraint to homes being among the last settings for deployment.

r004.rationale: The response describes commercial environments as narrow and says they teach robots little about the world; it does not claim commercial deployments provide substantial generalization without home deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the conventional wisdom is that you go commercial first, because warehouses and factories are structured, the ROI is clear, and the environment is forgiving. And I actually think that's backwards if your goal is general-purpose robots.

The home is the hardest environment there is. Every kitchen is different, objects are cluttered and deformable, there are kids and pets and lighting changes, and the tasks are open-ended. If you build for a warehouse, you end up overfitting to that structure, and you never collect the data that teaches a model how messy reality is. If you build for the home, the data you get is incredibly diverse, and that diversity is what makes a foundation model generalize. The home becomes a forcing function for capability.

The second piece is about the business. In commercial settings, you're competing against very optimized incumbents, specialized machines and people who've been doing the task for decades. The bar is "be cheaper than the current solution on day one." In the home, there's basically no incumbent for things like tidying, laundry, or loading a dishwasher. People will tolerate a robot that's slow and occasionally wrong, the same way people tolerated early Roombas, because the alternative is doing it themselves. That tolerance buys you time to improve.

And the third thing, which I think gets underrated, is the feedback loop. A home robot operates for hours a day and gets corrected by a real person who cares about the outcome. That's a continuous stream of grounded, labeled interaction. Commercial deployments give you volume on a narrow task; homes give you breadth with human feedback, and breadth is the bottleneck right now.

The honest counterargument is safety and cost. You can't ship something that hurts someone, and hardware is still expensive. So you start with tasks where failure is low-stakes, like picking things off the floor, and you design the system to be conservative. But I'd rather solve the hard problem directly and let the capabilities flow back into commercial settings, than solve the easy problem and hope it generalizes. Historically, that second path has not worked.

r001.rationale: It says home deployments yield incredibly diverse data and continuous grounded, labeled human feedback, which helps models generalize.

r002.rationale: It names safety as an honest counterargument and says a robot cannot be shipped if it might hurt someone.

r003.rationale: It cites expensive hardware as a counterargument to deploying robots in homes.

r004.rationale: It says commercial deployments provide volume on a narrow task and argues home deployment is needed for breadth; it does not claim commercial deployments alone provide substantial generalization.

astra-6.text:
I think the strongest case for the home is that there’s so much useful work to do there, and it’s a very diverse environment. If you could build a robot that helps with cooking, cleaning, or laundry across different homes, that would require a level of generalization that would be valuable in many other settings, too.

But I would separate that argument from the question of where you deploy first. Homes are really challenging. Every home is different, people have different preferences, and you’re operating around children, pets, and fragile objects. You also need the robot to be affordable and useful without someone constantly supervising it.

In a commercial setting, you can often narrow the task, structure the environment, and have someone available when the robot needs help. You can also measure the value pretty directly. So I think the home is a compelling goal, but that doesn’t necessarily make it the easiest starting point. The case for going there early would depend on finding a task that’s useful, sufficiently safe, and achievable with the capabilities you actually have.

r001.rationale: The response says home tasks could build useful generalization, but it does not cite access to valuable data as a reason to deploy there first.

r002.rationale: It describes safety challenges around children, pets, and fragile objects, but does not say these requirements make homes among the last settings for deployment.

r003.rationale: It says a home robot must be affordable, but does not connect a low price point to homes being among the last settings for deployment.

r004.rationale: It describes commercial settings as more structured and measurable, but does not say they can provide substantial generalization without home deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the strongest case for homes is that there’s a lot of valuable work to do there, and the environment forces you to confront generality. Every home is different. The objects are different, the layout is different, and what someone means by “clean up” can be different. If you can build a robot that’s useful across those variations, that’s a very powerful capability.

But I’d separate that argument from the question of where you deploy first. Homes are also difficult places to establish safety and reliability. You have people, pets, fragile objects, and a lot of situations you didn’t anticipate. In a commercial setting, you can often constrain the task, change the environment, and have someone available to intervene. That makes it easier to learn what actually breaks.

So, to me, the case for going into homes first depends on the scope. A robot doing one bounded, useful task in a home is a very different proposition from a robot that’s supposed to do all your chores. I’d want to understand what it can reliably do, how it handles failure, and whether the value it provides outweighs the supervision it needs. The home is a compelling destination, but that doesn’t automatically make it the best starting point.

r001.rationale: The response cites valuable work and the home environment’s variety, but does not present access to valuable data as a reason developers favor deploying there first.

r002.rationale: It says homes are difficult places to establish safety and reliability because of people, pets, fragile objects, and unforeseen situations, while commercial settings are easier to constrain. This identifies safety as a reason homes may not be an early deployment setting.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention a low price point as a reason to delay home deployment.

r004.rationale: The response says commercial settings make tasks easier to constrain and failures easier to learn from, but does not say commercial deployments provide substantial generalization without home deployment.
